## (a) One-particle basis and spin-singlet two-particle states

Let the periodic cubic lattice have L sites along each direction. The allowed dimensionless lattice momenta are qᵢ = 2πnᵢ/L, with nᵢ chosen from any complete set of L integers modulo L. For flavor f ∈ {n,p} and spin s ∈ {↑,↓}, define

a†_{qfs} = L⁻³ᐟ² ∑ᵣ exp(iq·r) n†_{rfs},    |q,f,s⟩ = a†_{qfs}|0⟩.

These states form an orthonormal one-particle basis. The free-particle dispersion following from the hopping term is

ε(q) = 2t ∑ᵢ₌ₓ,ᵧ,𝓏 [1 − cos(qᵢ)].

For two momenta q₁,q₂, the spin-singlet combination for ordered flavors f,g is

|q₁f;q₂g;S=0⟩ = 2⁻¹ᐟ² [a†_{q₁f↑}a†_{q₂g↓} − a†_{q₁f↓}a†_{q₂g↑}]|0⟩,

when the two terms represent distinct orthogonal Fock states. In particular, the neutron-neutron and proton-proton states are obtained by setting (f,g)=(n,n) and (p,p), respectively:

|nn;S=0⟩ ∝ [a†_{q₁n↑}a†_{q₂n↓} − a†_{q₁n↓}a†_{q₂n↑}]|0⟩,
|pp;S=0⟩ ∝ [a†_{q₁p↑}a†_{q₂p↓} − a†_{q₁p↓}a†_{q₂p↑}]|0⟩.

For an even-spatial-wave neutron-proton state, the flavor/isospin channel must also be specified. The symmetric I=1, I₃=0 combination is

|np;S=0,I=1,I₃=0⟩ = ½ [a†_{q₁n↑}a†_{q₂p↓} − a†_{q₁n↓}a†_{q₂p↑} + a†_{q₁p↑}a†_{q₂n↓} − a†_{q₁p↓}a†_{q₂n↑}]|0⟩,

for distinct modes as written. Fermionic anticommutation determines the normalization in coincident-mode cases. For example, the nn expression with q₁=q₂=0 is proportional to a†_{0n↑}a†_{0n↓}|0⟩ and should be normalized as that Fock state, rather than using the distinct-state normalization factor. For identical nucleons, the antisymmetric spin singlet requires a symmetric spatial wavefunction.

With the specified ordering N=(n↑,n↓,p↑,p↓)ᵀ, the displayed contact term is Ct n†↑n†↓n↓n↑. Thus it acts directly only on an onsite neutron-neutron pair in the spin-singlet channel; proton-proton or neutron-proton contact interactions would require additional terms.

## (b) Matching t to the physical box

The literal lowest free-particle mode is q=0 and has energy zero. The requested nonzero-energy matching therefore uses the lowest nonzero mode, with one component q=2π/L and the other two zero. Its lattice energy is

ε₁(lattice) = 2t[1 − cos(2π/L)].

In a physical periodic box of length L_phy, the corresponding lowest nonzero momentum is p=2π/L_phy, with nonrelativistic kinetic energy p²/(2M_phy), in units ℏ=c=1. Equating the two gives the exact finite-lattice result

t = (2π/L_phy)² / {4M_phy[1 − cos(2π/L)]}
  = π² / {2M_phy L_phy² sin²(π/L)}.

If a=L_phy/L is the lattice spacing, then for L large, 1−cos(2π/L) ≃ 2π²/L², and hence

t → 1/(2M_phy a²).

This is the usual continuum-limit hopping coefficient; the exact finite-L expression above is the result before taking that limit.

## (c) Lowest nonzero single-particle energy

For L_phy=3.4 fm and M_phy=1634 MeV, restore ℏc=197.32698 MeV·fm to evaluate the momentum in MeV:

E₁ = [2π(ℏc)/L_phy]²/(2M_phy)
   = [2π(197.32698 MeV·fm)/(3.4 fm)]²/(2·1634 MeV)
   ≃ 40.7 MeV.

The six momentum vectors (±1,0,0), (0,±1,0), and (0,0,±1), in units of 2π/L_phy, form the lowest nonzero momentum shell. This is the continuum energy above the rest energy in the nonrelativistic model.

## (d) Binding condition, coupling, and first excited state

Let B=|E_B|=17.8 MeV and U=Ct. In the total-momentum-zero two-particle sector, the relative free energy is 2ε(q). The contact-interaction bound-state equation on a specified lattice regulator is

1/(Ct) = −∫_BZ d³q/(2π)³ · 1/[B+2ε(q)],

where ε(q)=2t∑ᵢ[1−cos(qᵢ)] and the integral is over the lattice Brillouin zone. Equivalently,

1/C = −∫_BZ d³q/(2π)³ · 1/[B/t+4∑ᵢ(1−cos(qᵢ))].

This shows why the information given does not determine a numerical bare lattice C: the result depends on t, or equivalently on the lattice spacing/ultraviolet cutoff. The problem specifies the physical box length but not the lattice spacing or number of lattice sites. Taking L→∞ at fixed lattice spacing makes the momentum sum an integral but does not remove this cutoff dependence. Taking a→0 is a different limit and requires a regulator-dependent renormalization of the bare coupling. For example, a sharp-cutoff continuum contact interaction also gives a bare coupling that depends explicitly on its cutoff Λ. A numerical C therefore cannot be supplied without an additional regulator and lattice-spacing prescription.

Under the additional zero-range continuum assumption, the binding energy does fix the inverse bound-state size κ and the corresponding scattering length:

κ = √(M_phy B) = √(1634·17.8) MeV ≃ 170.5 MeV,
a_s = 1/κ ≃ 1.16 fm,

where the last conversion uses ℏc. These are continuum quantities, not a unique value of the lattice bare C.

In infinite volume, the bound state at −17.8 MeV is followed by a scattering continuum with relative energies E(k)=k²/M_phy ≥ 0. The continuum threshold at zero is not a discrete first excited eigenstate. Thus there is no discrete first excited-state energy in the stated infinite-volume limit; the continuum begins at zero.

## (e) Second excited state and degeneracy

For the same reason, there is no discrete second excited level or finite level degeneracy in the infinite-volume limit: the unbound two-particle spectrum is continuous. Its states can be labeled by relative momentum and, when useful, angular-momentum quantum numbers. A finite box would discretize these states, but their energies and degeneracies would then depend on the box size and on the interaction/regulator details. Those details are not supplied, so a unique second excited energy or degeneracy cannot be calculated from the question as stated.

In particular, L→∞ (the thermodynamic limit at fixed lattice spacing) is not equivalent to a→0 (the continuum limit). Neither permits one to infer the requested discrete excited levels without specifying an appropriate finite-volume setup; and a numerical bare C also requires the ultraviolet regulator or lattice spacing.
